**Rick Douglas Husband** (July 12, 1957– February 1, 2003) was an American [astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut") and [fighter pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighter_pilot "Fighter pilot"). He traveled into space twice: as pilot of [STS-96](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-96 "STS-96") and commander of [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"). Husband and the rest of the crew of STS-107 were killed when _Columbia_[disintegrated during reentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") into the [Earth's atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_atmosphere "Earth's atmosphere"). He is also a recipient of the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor").

## Early life, education and training

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rick_Husband&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life, education and training")]

Husband was born on July 12, 1957, in [Amarillo, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amarillo,_Texas "Amarillo, Texas").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Husband#cite_note-NASA_Bio-1) At age 17, he earned his pilot's license while flying out of [Tradewind Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tradewind_Airport "Tradewind Airport"). Husband graduated with honors from [Amarillo High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amarillo_High_School "Amarillo High School") in 1975.

Husband earned a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [mechanical engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanical_engineering "Mechanical engineering") from [Texas Tech University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Tech_University "Texas Tech University") in 1980 after five years of study. He earned his [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degree from [Fresno State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresno_State_University "Fresno State University"). Upon graduation, Husband was commissioned as a pilot in the [United States Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force"), having been enrolled in [ROTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ROTC "ROTC") his last two years of college. Husband underwent pilot training at [Vance Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vance_Air_Force_Base "Vance Air Force Base"), in [Enid, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enid,_Oklahoma "Enid, Oklahoma"). This was followed by Land Survival School at [Fairchild Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Air_Force_Base "Fairchild Air Force Base"), in [Spokane, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spokane,_Washington "Spokane, Washington"), and [Fighter Lead-in School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trainer_aircraft#Lead-in_fighter_training "Trainer aircraft") in New Mexico. After he got married on February 27, 1982, Husband trained in the [F-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-4 "F-4") at [Homestead Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homestead_Air_Force_Base "Homestead Air Force Base") next.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Husband#cite_note-Rick-2)

## U.S. Air Force career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rick_Husband&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: U.S. Air Force career")]

Husband was assigned to a squadron at [Moody Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moody_Air_Force_Base "Moody Air Force Base") in [Valdosta, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valdosta,_Georgia "Valdosta, Georgia"), flying the F-4E. He then transferred to [George AFB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_AFB "George AFB"), in [Victorville, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorville,_California "Victorville, California") in December 1985, where Husband became an F-4 instructor. By then, he had accumulated 1000 hours of flying time.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Husband#cite_note-Rick-2):30,32

In December 1987, Husband was assigned to [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") in [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), where he attended the [USAF Test Pilot School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USAF_Test_Pilot_School "USAF Test Pilot School") class 88A along with future [Canadian Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Space_Agency "Canadian Space Agency") astronaut [Chris Hadfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Hadfield "Chris Hadfield"). Upon completion of test pilot school, Husband served as a test pilot flying the F-4 and all five models of the [F-15 Eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-15_Eagle "F-15 Eagle"). In the F-15 Combined Test Force, he was the program manager for the [Pratt & Whitney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pratt_&_Whitney "Pratt & Whitney")[F100-PW-229](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pratt_&_Whitney_F100#F100-PW-229 "Pratt & Whitney F100") increased performance engine and also served as the F-15 Aerial Demonstration Pilot.

In June 1992, Husband was assigned to the Aircraft and Armament Evaluation Establishment at [Boscombe Down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boscombe_Down "Boscombe Down"), England, as an exchange test pilot with the [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force"). At Boscombe Down, he was the Tornado GR1 and GR4 Project Pilot and served as a test pilot in the Hawk, Hunter, Buccaneer, Jet Provost, Tucano, and Harvard.

Husband logged over 3,800 hours of flight time in more than 40 different types of [aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft "Aircraft").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Husband#cite_note-NASA_Bio-1)

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rick_Husband&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: NASA career")]

Husband was selected as an astronaut candidate by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") in December 1994, the same week he was promoted to lieutenant colonel.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Husband#cite_note-Rick-2):67 Husband reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in March 1995 to begin a year of training and evaluation. Upon completion of training, he was named the Astronaut Office representative for Advanced Projects at Johnson Space Center, working on [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") Upgrades, the [Crew Return Vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crew_Return_Vehicle "Crew Return Vehicle") (CRV) and studies to return to the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon") and travel to [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars"). Husband eventually served as Chief of Safety for the [Astronaut Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut_Office "Astronaut Office"). In 1999, he flew as pilot on [STS-96](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-96 "STS-96") and logged 235 hours and 13 minutes in [space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_space "Outer space"). Husband was later assigned to command the crew of [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"), which was launched early in 2003. Along with the rest of the STS-107 crew, he was killed upon reentry when the shuttle disintegrated over Texas.
